---
title: "Research"
subtitle: "How soil life adapts, persists and records human history, read through its DNA"
---

I study soil animals, mostly earthworms and other macrofauna, and the microbes that live in and around them, from single genes to whole genomes, metagenomes and transcriptomes. The questions come from the field: what lives in a soil, how it copes with extreme or changing conditions, and what that tells us about the soil's health and history. The work runs from sampling in Portuguese farms, Azorean volcanoes and the Amazon to the wet lab and the command line, and since 2025 it is the core of the [Environmental Genomics Laboratory (EnGeL)](https://envigenomics.eu/research.html) at the University of Coimbra.

{{< include _gen/research_figures.md >}}

## Soil biodiversity you can measure

Soil holds a large share of the planet's species, yet most soil-health monitoring still leaves soil animals out because identifying them by eye is slow and depends on a few specialists. I develop and test DNA-based approaches (COI barcoding, metabarcoding and integrative morphological–molecular taxonomy) that make soil fauna countable and comparable across sites and countries, and I lead the work on soil-health assessment approaches (work package 4) in the Horizon Europe project BENCHMARKS, which is building harmonised indicators for European soil monitoring.

Key outputs:

- Fraga Dornellas et al. (2025) [DNA-based strategies for soil biodiversity assessment: insights from carabid beetles](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.72461). *Ecology and Evolution*.
- Jänsch et al. (2025) [Morphological and DNA-based identification of earthworm communities compared](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.71155). *Ecology and Evolution*.
- White et al. (2020) [Methods and approaches to advance soil macroecology](https://doi.org/10.1111/geb.13156). *Global Ecology and Biogeography*.
- Leitão et al. (2026) [Rapid evidence mapping of soil fauna responses to agricultural management assisted by large language models](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.geoderma.2026.117890). *Geoderma*.

## Humans written into the soil

The Amazonian Dark Earths (*terra preta*) are fertile soils created by pre-Columbian people and still distinct centuries later. With archaeologists and soil scientists I have shown that they carry their own biological signature: different earthworm and macroinvertebrate communities, and ecosystem engineers such as the peregrine earthworm *Pontoscolex corethrurus*, whose genetics mirror human movement across the tropics. The same questions now feed practical work on *terra preta*-inspired amendments for degraded tropical soils.

Key outputs:

- Lombardo et al. (2022) [Evidence confirms an anthropic origin of Amazonian Dark Earths](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-31064-2). *Nature Communications*.
- Demetrio et al. (2021) [A "dirty" footprint: macroinvertebrate diversity in Amazonian anthropic soils](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.15752). *Global Change Biology*.
- Leitão et al. (2026) [Soil, root and earthworm-gut microbiomes under *terra preta*-inspired amendments](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apsoil.2026.107278). *Applied Soil Ecology*.
- Taheri et al. (2018) [Complex taxonomy of the peregrine earthworm *Pontoscolex corethrurus*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ympev.2018.02.021). *Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution*.

## Life on the volcanic edge

Volcanic and geothermal soils combine heat, acidity, CO₂ and metals, a natural laboratory for adaptation to several stresses at once. In the Azores I showed that earthworms living in degassing soils are genetically isolated from neighbouring populations, and with colleagues I have followed adaptation in genomes, transcriptomes and physiology, from volcanic fumaroles to high-altitude soils.

Key outputs:

- Cunha et al. (2014) [Living on a volcano's edge: genetic isolation of an extremophile terrestrial metazoan](https://doi.org/10.1038/hdy.2013.84). *Heredity*.
- Perry et al. (2022) [Molecular insights into high-altitude adaptation of *Aporrectodea caliginosa*](https://doi.org/10.26508/lsa.202201513). *Life Science Alliance*.
- Novo et al. (2014) [The functional ghost in the genome machine: environmentally induced changes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.toxlet.2014.06.095). *Toxicology Letters*.

## Farming, chemicals and soil life

Pesticides, their tank mixtures, biofertilisers, sludge and plastics reach soils together. In Horizon Europe and EFSA projects (SYBERAC, EESE, VALERECO, GOOD, PARC) I combine ecotoxicology with community and microbiome sequencing to see how these pressures change soil organisms and their functions, and what that means for risk assessment and for farming that keeps soils alive.

Key outputs:

- Lori et al. (2025) [Response of soil biota to agricultural management practices: a quantitative meta-dataset](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.soilbio.2025.109815). *Soil Biology and Biochemistry*.
- da Silva et al. (2021) [Pesticides in no-tillage farming systems and surrounding forest patches in Brazil](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-88779-3). *Scientific Reports*.
- Quigley et al. (2024) [Pristine and UV-aged polyethylene microplastics, earthworm gut microbiome and reproduction](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ejsobi.2024.103640). *European Journal of Soil Biology*.

## Toolkit

Across these lines the same set of methods comes back: field sampling design and integrative taxonomy; DNA and RNA work, qPCR and library preparation; short- and long-read sequencing (Illumina and Oxford Nanopore); genome, metagenome and transcriptome assembly and annotation; population genomics and phylogenomics; and reproducible analysis in R and on Linux/HPC. The lab's protocols are open in the [EnGeL protocol handbook](https://luiscunhamx.github.io/EnGeL-Repository/).
